questions.q: A script is run as `./deploy.sh web-01 production`. What does `$2` contain?
questions.explain: $1 is the first argument (web-01) and $2 is the second (production). $0 would be the script name itself.

questions.q: What does `$#` give you inside a script?
options: The number of arguments the script was called with
The exit status of the last command
The full text of all arguments combined
questions.explain: $# expands to the count of positional parameters passed to the script (or function).

questions.q: In `while [ "$#" -gt 0 ]; do echo "$1"; shift; done`, what does `shift` do on each pass?
options: Drops the current $1 and renumbers the remaining arguments down by one, so the old $2 becomes the new $1
Deletes all remaining arguments at once
Reverses the order of the arguments
questions.explain: shift removes $1 from the argument list and shifts every remaining argument's number down by one, which is what lets a loop work through all of them.

questions.q: Why use `read -s` instead of plain `read` when prompting for a deploy token?
options: read -s hides the typed input from the screen, instead of echoing it as the user types
read -s only works for numeric input
read -s automatically encrypts the stored value
questions.explain: The -s flag suppresses terminal echo while typing, which is the standard way to prompt for sensitive input like a password or token.

questions.q: In `getopts "e:v" opt`, what does the colon after `e` mean?
options: The -e flag is required to appear first
The -e flag expects a value, which getopts places in $OPTARG
The colon has no effect on parsing
questions.explain: In a getopts option string, a colon after a letter means that flag takes an argument, available afterward in $OPTARG. A letter with no colon (like v here) is a plain on/off flag.
